The many Tartarys in motion

Turn the dial

26 old maps laid on the real earth, from 1516 to 1894. Drag the wheel and watch where each mapmaker lettered the word Tartary and what ground he gave it: it arrives, swells, splits, shrinks and is gone. Lift the sheet and the outline stays behind on today's map.

1253 to 1255 · William of Rubruck · No map: a journey

A people, not yet a place

William of Rubruck rides from the Black Sea to the Mongol court at Karakorum and back, and writes of the Tartars as a people on the move, with their tents, carts and herds. The line is his road. On the world maps of his century in this atlas, the word is not yet lettered as a country.

Ride his roadMeet the witness

The line joins the stops of his journey. It is not the exact road.

about 1300 · Hereford Cathedral · The Hereford world map

The great wall maps do not know the name

The largest medieval world map to survive was drawn while the first reports from the Mongol courts were already in Europe, yet it carries none of them. Its northern Asia is still Scythia, with Gog and Magog walled in by Alexander. It is a round picture of the world with east at the top, so it cannot be laid on the real earth. Open it to see.

Open this map

about 1450 · Unknown maker · The Borgia world map

The word reaches the maps

One of the earliest maps to letter Tartaria as a region, with a note explaining it and little pictures of Tartar wagon camps, and with Gog and Magog set close by. It is engraved on a round metal plate with south at the top, so it cannot be laid on the real earth either. Open it to see.

1516 · Martin Waldseemüller · Carta marina, sheet 3

Three Tartarys around the Caspian

[Carta marina navigatoria Portugallen navigationes ...] sheet 3

This sheet letters TARTARIA three times. The largest stands on the steppe north of the Caspian Sea, over the tent of the khan, and two more east of the Caspian are tied to older country names: TARTARIA CORASINE (Khwarezm) and TARTARIA TORQVESTEN (Turkestan). North of the Sea of Azov the plain is called CAMPESTRIA TARTAR, and note after note across the sheet says that Russians, Armenians and Persians live under the Tartars.

The whole sheet at the Library of CongressThis map in the atlas

Laid on the earth by 39 matched places. Left out one at a time, a place lands about 182 km from where it belongs; the worst lands 596 km off. That is the mapmaker's error, kept on purpose.

What is uncertain (7 notes)
  • The heading TERRA MONGAL ET QUE VERA TARTARIA DICITUR is not on this sheet; it must stand on the neighbouring sheet to the east (sheet 4), which is a different picture. The title given here is only the running head printed over this sheet, and the map's main title stands on another sheet.
  • The western two thirds can be laid on the earth honestly: the Black Sea, the Levant coast, Russia and the west and north of the Caspian come from sea charts and reports and fit to within a few hundred km. The sheet sits turned about 40 degrees, which is only the projection at this far western longitude, not a fault.
  • East of the Caspian not one place can be matched: there is no Samarkand, Bukhara or Urgench, and the country is drawn from Ptolemy with rivers and old province names. The eastern third, where TARTARIA CORASINE and TARTARIA TORQVESTEN stand, is carried along by the western fit, so its position on the earth is only a rough guide.
  • The Caspian is drawn as an oval lying east to west, as on the old sea charts, so its true north to south shape cannot be matched. The places around it (Volga delta, Kura mouth, Ural mouth, south shore) pull against each other.
  • Several place readings are not sure: Sarai is read from the town lettered Sala ciuit. on the Volga, the river name dayr fl. is read as the Yaik (Ural), and Grassan is read as Kashan. Derbent could not be found by name, Astrakhan is lettered only as agitarcam in a list of names at the Volga delta, and CASANA (Kazan) is lettered as a country near the Don with no town sign.
  • The second line of CAMPESTRIA TARTAR reads TAR TAR and seems cut short (for Tartarorum or Tartarie). A small name east of the Sea of Azov, Tacaria over Tarmacho, may be a slip for Tartaria but is lettered with a c, so it was not marked; nor were the many written notes that name the Tartars, such as sub mandato Tartarorum and sub tributo tartarorum.
  • None of the four Tartary names on this sheet has a drawn border, so the outlines shown are our reading of the lettering, carried out to the nearest rivers, mountain chains and shores; the south side of the large TARTARIA, set halfway to the name CVMANIE, and the west end of TARTARIA CORASINE at the Caspian shore are the least sure.

1562 · Anthony Jenkinson · Russia, Muscovy and Tartary

One word, letter by letter, across the steppe

RVSSIAE, MOSCOVIAE ET TARTARIAE DESCRIPTIO. Auctore Antonio Ienkensono Anglo, edita Londini Anno 1562 & dedicata illustriss. D. Henrico Sydneo Wallie…

The word TARTARIA is lettered once, in big letters spread one by one across the open steppe from the Don and lower Volga eastward past the Yaik toward the country above Tashkent. It is not divided into parts; smaller names such as Nagaia, Cassacki, Turkmen and Kirges sit inside and around it, and the far north is given to the Samoyeds instead. A note beside Samarkand calls that city the former capital of all Tartary.

The whole sheet at the Library of CongressThis map in the atlas

Laid on the earth by 47 matched places. Left out one at a time, a place lands about 127 km from where it belongs; the worst lands 676 km off. That is the mapmaker's error, kept on purpose.

What is uncertain (5 notes)
  • The picture used is a 1914 black and white Russian reproduction that follows Ortelius's 1570 reduced plate, not the 1562 London sheet. Fine lettering is blurred in places.
  • The word also appears in the title and inside two written notes, the one at Samarkand and one saying Little Khorasan was taken 'adiuvantibus Tartaris 1558'. These are blocks of text and were not marked.
  • The Ob, Sibir, Tashkent and Kashgar came from hearsay and sit far from their true places. The Caspian is drawn wider east to west than north to south, so its shore towns fit badly.
  • Vardo and Kola are read from a dark, crowded coast, so their spots may be slightly off.
  • The map draws no border for Tartaria. The outline shown is our reading of where the spread letters reach, closed off by the nearest rivers, the Caspian shore and the dotted limits of the neighbouring provinces, and the map's own note at Samarkand suggests the name was meant to reach further south-east.

1570 · Abraham Ortelius · Tartary, or the kingdom of the Great Khan

The Great Khan's whole realm under one word

TARTARIAE SIVE MAGNI CHAMI REGNI typus

Ortelius letters TARTARIA once, in large capitals across the steppe north-east of the Caspian, and adds in small script that it takes in Asiatic Sarmatia and both Scythias of the ancient writers. He does not divide it into Great, Little or Chinese Tartary; the rest of the country is filled with the names of hordes and with Marco Polo's kingdoms such as Tangut, Camul, Tenduc and Cathay, all of them, by the title and the note in the lower cartouche, under the Great Khan.

The whole sheet at the Library of CongressThis map in the atlas

Laid on the earth by 35 matched places. Left out one at a time, a place lands about 247 km from where it belongs; the worst lands 1,502 km off. That is the mapmaker's error, kept on purpose.

What is uncertain (7 notes)
  • The word Tartary also occurs inside blocks of text that were not marked: the title cartouche (TARTARIAE SIVE MAGNI CHAMI REGNI typus), the lower left cartouche ('Continet hec tabula oem Tartariam'), the note by the Great Khan's tent ('lingua Tartarorum') and the Altai note ('oes Tartarie imperatores').
  • A town on the China coast is lettered Tartaho. It is a town name, not the word Tartary, and was not marked.
  • The interior east of Samarkand and the whole north-east coast (Scythicum prom., Tabin, Arsareth, the Strait of Anian) are legend, so nothing fixes the sheet there. The fit rests on the Black Sea, the Caspian, the Russian north coast to the Ob, the China coast and Japan.
  • No fitting place could be found in the south-west and south, where Persia and India are covered by a cartouche and blank lettering, so that side is held only by Tabriz, Merv and Termez. Moscow and Bukhara are not on this sheet, Canton lies off the bottom edge, and Korea and Novaya Zemlya are not drawn.
  • The Caspian is drawn as an east to west oval and Hangzhou (Quinsai) far north of Ningbo, so those places land far off however the sheet is laid.
  • Merv, Termez and Margilan are read from Gastaldi-style names (Maru, Terment, Merglan) and are not sure.
  • The outline for Tartary is not a border drawn on the sheet. It follows the rivers, lake, mountains and coasts that the small text at lower left names as the limits of the Great Khan's empire, so it takes in Cathay and Mangi, and its south side is partly a judged line.

about 1600 · Arnoldo di Arnoldi · Map of Asia

One word across the north of Asia

ASIA

Arnoldi letters TARTARIA once, in the largest capitals on the sheet, spread in two groups of letters (TAR and TARIA) across the north of Asia from east of the Ob to a gulf of the northern sea. He draws no border round it and does not split it into Great, Little or Chinese Tartary. A long Italian note between the two groups of letters describes the land of the Tartars as dry, windy, short of towns and mostly Muslim. Around the name he letters hordes in the north, Turchestan, Maurenaher and Zagatai towards the Caspian Sea, and Marco Polo's Bargu, Tangut, Cataio and Mangi towards China, with Moscovia, Russia, Casan and Astracan on the west.

The whole sheet at the Library of Congress

Laid on the earth by 77 matched places. Left out one at a time, a place lands about 242 km from where it belongs; the worst lands 969 km off. That is the mapmaker's error, kept on purpose.

What is uncertain (6 notes)
  • This copy shows no date and no maker's name. Arnoldi, Florimi of Siena and the date of about 1600 come from the Library of Congress catalogue.
  • The sheet draws no border round Tartary and has no colour. The outline shown is a reading of where the letters lie, carried to the nearest coast and rivers.
  • The outline leaves Tangut and Cathay outside. A reader in 1600 might have counted them as part of Tartary; the sheet does not say.
  • The far north-east of the sheet is drawn from legend and from Marco Polo, with no real places to pin it down. The second half of the name lies there, so its place on the modern map is rough.
  • The word Tartar also appears in a long note on the sheet about the land of the Tartars. It is not marked as a label.
  • The Caspian Sea, the Sea of Azov and Delhi are badly placed on the sheet itself, so they land far from their true spots.

1626 · John Speed · Asia with the islands adjoining

The name reaches the Arctic sea

ASIA with the Islands adioyning described, the atire of the people, & Townes of importance, all of them newly augmented by I

Speed letters TARTARIA in large spaced capitals across the country between the Volga and the Ob, running up from north of the Caspian Sea. The word comes back three more times: as a tribe (Kaski Tartari) in the steppe below it, as a town called Tartar in the empty far north-east, and on the water as The Tartarian Sea along the whole Arctic coast. A note beside the Great Wall says it was built against sudden inroads of the Tartars, and one of the costume figures in the border is labelled Tartarian.

The whole sheet at the Library of Congress

Laid on the earth by 39 matched places. Left out one at a time, a place lands about 223 km from where it belongs; the worst lands 1,010 km off. That is the mapmaker's error, kept on purpose.

What is uncertain (7 notes)
  • The tribe name under TARTARIA has a meridian line through its third letter. It is read here as 'Kaski Tartari' (long s, probably the Kazakhs); earlier notes gave 'Kalbi Tartari', and 'Kalki' is also possible.
  • The note on the Great Wall and the border figure lettered TARTARIAN hold the word, but they are a text note and a border decoration, so they were not marked.
  • North-east Asia is drawn by guess (Mongul, Tenduc, Tartar, a coast running to a strait with America), so nothing fixes the fit there beyond Beijing and northern Japan.
  • The Caspian is the old east to west oval, and Samarkand is set far east. Both are true places that the mapmaker misplaced.
  • The picture is a photograph of an open book, with a gutter and some page curve, and the plate edge is slightly out of square.
  • The town marks for Mogadishu and Macao are slightly uncertain.
  • The sheet draws no border round TARTARIA, so its outline here is judged from the lettering and the nearest rivers and coasts: the Volga on the west, the Arctic coast on the north, the first river and lakes beyond the last letter on the east, and the Caspian and the river running into it on the south. Speed may have meant the name to reach further east, where he puts a town called Tartar and writes of Tartars beyond the Great Wall.

about 1657 · Willem Blaeu · Wall map of Asia

One word from the Volga to Cathay

NOVA ET EXACTA ASIÆ GEOGRAPHICA DESCRIPTIO, auct

Blaeu letters TARTARIA once, in the largest capitals on the land, one letter at a time from west of the Volga across the Ob to the kingdom of Tangut, with no border line round it. Under it he names Tartar peoples (the Kazakh Tartars and the Kalmuks, "that is, long-haired Tartars"), a Chagatai Tartary by Bukhara, and north of the Black Sea "Crimea, or Perekop Tartary". There is no Siberia as a country, only the town Sibier on the Ob; the north is RUSSIA, SAMOIEDA, Lucomorye and Yugra, and the far east is filled with Marco Polo's names (Tangut, Tenduc, Mongul, Cathay with Cambalu) and a town and river called Tartar. A note on the Great Wall says it was built against the raids of the Tartars, and the printed text in the border calls the country "the empire of the Great Cham, or Tartary".

The whole sheet at the Library of Congress

Laid on the earth by 74 matched places. Left out one at a time, a place lands about 214 km from where it belongs; the worst lands 955 km off. That is the mapmaker's error, kept on purpose.

What is uncertain (6 notes)
  • The date is not printed on the sheet. About 1657 is the Library of Congress's estimate for this issue by Nicolaes Visscher; Blaeu first made the map about fifty years earlier.
  • The sheet draws no border round TARTARIA, so its outline here is judged from the lettering and the nearest coasts, rivers and the Great Wall. The stretch from the Wall to the Oxus river and the stretch between the Volga and the Ob are the least certain.
  • North-east Asia is drawn by guess from Marco Polo and older maps (Tenduc, Cathay with Cambalu, a town called Tartar, the Strait of Anian), so the east end of TARTARIA cannot be placed firmly on the real earth.
  • ZAGATAY Tart. is cut short on the sheet, so it may mean a country (Tartaria) or a people (Tartari).
  • Several notes on the map and the printed text and a costume picture in the border also use the word; they were read but not marked.
  • Some true places sit far from where they belong because the mapmaker misplaced them: Beijing, Delhi, Kashgar, northern Japan and the east shore of the Caspian.

about 1680 · Frederick de Wit · Great Tartary, the Mogul empire, Japan and China

Great Tartary, from the Ob to the Pacific

MAGNÆ TARTARIÆ, MAGNI MOGOLIS IMPERII, IAPONIÆ et CHINÆ, Nova Descriptio

The words TARTARIA MAGNA, Great Tartary, are spread one letter at a time across the whole of inner Asia, from the river Ob to the Pacific coast and from the Arctic shore down to the Great Wall of China. Inside that space the sheet names many separate peoples and kingdoms, among them the Kazakh Tartars, Chagatai, Turkestan, the Mongols, Cathay and Tangut, and the Arctic sea above is called the Tartar Sea. Siberia is only a small name by the Ob, and the far north-east is filled with names from Marco Polo and from legend, such as Magog and a town and river called Tartar.

The whole sheet at the Library of CongressThis map in the atlas

Laid on the earth by 49 matched places. Left out one at a time, a place lands about 163 km from where it belongs; the worst lands 980 km off. That is the mapmaker's error, kept on purpose.

What is uncertain (7 notes)
  • Short Latin notes on the map body also use the word and were not marked: 'Castrum contra irruptionem Tartarorum', 'eunt ac redeunt Tartari' and 'Regnum Tartariae Sepulchra sunt', besides a note on the trumpeters.
  • 'Tart.' after ZACATAY is cut short on the sheet, so it may mean Tartaria or Tartari.
  • North of China and east of the Ob almost nothing on the sheet is real: the Arctic and north-east coasts are guesses, there is no Baikal, Aral or Amur, and the towns come from Marco Polo. The fit there rests on the Ob and Yenisei mouths and on the Dutch survey of Yezo and Sakhalin at the east edge, so the place of the TARTARIA lettering on the earth is loose.
  • The Volga mouth and Astrakhan fall off the left edge, so the west side is held by the Ural river mouth, Samara, Saratov and Bolgar.
  • Tashkent is lettered far to the east of Samarkand and was kept out of the fit.
  • Two places stay far off because the sheet itself is wrong there: Verkhoturye (about 1000 km off) and the south-east corner of the Caspian (about 500 km off).
  • The sheet has no line marked as the edge of Great Tartary. Its outline here is what is left between the dashed borders engraved for Russia, Persia, the Mogul empire, China and Korea, so Tibet, Turkestan and Samarkand fall inside it.

1700 · Guillaume Delisle · Map of Asia

One Great Tartary, split by ruler

L'Asie, dressée sur les observations de l'Academie Royale des Sciences et quelques autres, et sur les memoires les plus recens. Par G. de l'Isle…

Delisle letters GRANDE TARTARIE once, in the largest capitals of inner Asia, in a single line from the Volga to the Amur, and then splits that ground by who rules it. Engraved dotted lines mark off TARTARIE MOSCOVITE across the north from the White Sea to the Yenisei and Lake Baikal, TARTARIE INDEPENDANTE from the Caspian to the Mongols (its line also takes in the kingdoms of Tibet), and TARTARIE CHINOISE north of the Great Wall, which carries TARTARIE OCCIDENTALE and TARTARIE OR.LE (Orientale) inside it. PETITE TARTARIE stands apart on the steppe north of the Black Sea, with the Crimea. Inside these he letters peoples and countries of their own, such as SIBERIE, the Samoyeds, Ostyaks, Tungus and Yakuts, the Kalmyks, Uzbeks, TURQUESTAN and the Mongols, and no people on the sheet is called Tartars.

The whole sheet at the Library of Congress

Laid on the earth by 110 matched places. Left out one at a time, a place lands about 119 km from where it belongs; the worst lands 1,309 km off. That is the mapmaker's error, kept on purpose.

What is uncertain (6 notes)
  • The sheet is dated 1700, but the address on it (Quai de l'Horloge) suggests this copy was printed some years later from the same plate.
  • Great Tartary has no border of its own here. Its outline is the three ruled parts put together and carried to the coast, which is a reading of where the big letters lie.
  • The line round Independent Tartary also takes in Tibet, though the name is lettered far to the north of it. The sheet does not say whether Tibet was meant to count as Tartary.
  • Muscovite Tartary is drawn as the whole compartment inside the engraved line, from the White Sea and the Volga to Lake Baikal. The Yakut country and the far north-east are outside that line on this sheet, even though Russia held them.
  • The dotted line used to part Western from Eastern Tartary is not labelled on the sheet.
  • North-east Siberia, the Lena, the Amur mouth and Lake Baikal are drawn from hearsay and sit hundreds of kilometres out of place, so the outlines are rough on today's map in that corner.

Other big names in the same country

1706 · Guillaume Delisle · Map of Tartary

Split in three by who rules it

Carte de Tartarie, dressée sur les relations de plusieurs voyageurs de differentes nations et sur quelques observations qui ont été faites dans ce…

Delisle uses Tartary as the name for nearly all of northern and central Asia and splits it by who rules it: Muscovite Tartary across the whole of Siberia, Independent Tartary over the Kalmyk and Uzbek country east of the Caspian, and Chinese Tartary from the Mongol lands to the Pacific, with Western and Eastern Tartary lettered inside the Chinese part. Little Tartary sits apart on the steppe north of the Crimea. Within these broad names the sheet letters kingdoms and peoples of its own, such as the Kingdom of Siberia, the Kalmyks and the Mongols, and it names three smaller groups as Tartars: those of Tyumen, of the Kuban and of Dagestan.

The whole sheet at the Library of CongressThis map in the atlas

Laid on the earth by 40 matched places. Left out one at a time, a place lands about 276 km from where it belongs; the worst lands 1,103 km off. That is the mapmaker's error, kept on purpose.

What is uncertain (5 notes)
  • North-east Siberia is drawn from hearsay: the Lena, Yakutsk and the Amur mouth sit six to seven degrees too far south and the coast beyond the Lena is guesswork. The fit is poor there, with errors of 800 to 1100 km, though the places themselves are certain.
  • Lake Baikal is drawn very small and the Angara towns are crowded against it, so Irkutsk lands about 750 km off.
  • Novaya Zemlya is joined to the mainland and no Kamchatka is drawn, so there are no sound fitting points on the far northern and north-eastern edges beyond the Yenisei mouth and the Tugur mouth.
  • The first T of TARTARIE MOSCOVITE, just west of the Urals near Solikamsk, is half hidden by the border colour and reads almost like an I. Its position is taken from the spacing of the letters.
  • The lower left corner is taken up by the title cartouche, so the south-west has no fitting points below Derbent and west of Khiva.

about 1710 · Johann Baptist Homann · Map of Asia

Great Tartary written across green and pink

Asiae Recentissima Delineatio, Qua Status et Imperia Totius Orientis unacum Orientalibus Indiis exhibentur Authore Io. Bapt. Homanno Norimbergae

The largest name in the north is TARTARIA MAGNA, Great Tartary. Its letters start east of the Caspian Sea, cross the green land and carry on over the pink land of Siberia to the eastern sea. Inside the green land a second, smaller name reads TARTARIA VAGABUNDORUM INDEPENDENS, the independent Tartary of the wandering peoples, with Kalmyks, Black and Yellow Mongolia, Chagatai and the Uzbeks lettered in it. The yellow land north of the Great Wall is called CHINA EXTRA MUROS SIVE TARTARIA CHINENSIS, China outside the walls or Chinese Tartary, and TARTARIA MINOR, Little Tartary, sits north of the Black Sea. The pink north is lettered SIBERIA and MOSCOVITICUM, so the Russian lands and Great Tartary overlap on this sheet; the Arctic sea north of the Lena is MARE TARTARICUM GLACIALE, and a people called CIRCASSI TARTARI stand north of the Caucasus.

The whole sheet at the Library of Congress

Laid on the earth by 86 matched places. Left out one at a time, a place lands about 190 km from where it belongs; the worst lands 790 km off. That is the mapmaker's error, kept on purpose.

What is uncertain (5 notes)
  • The sheet has no printed year. About 1710 is a reasoned guess: after 1704, before Homann became Imperial Geographer in 1715.
  • Great Tartary has no drawn border here. The outline shown is our reading of how far the letters spread.
  • The green, pink and yellow were painted by hand on this copy, and other copies may be coloured differently.
  • The mapmaker drew Siberia, the Caspian Sea and Japan badly out of shape, so the outlines land only roughly on the real earth.
  • Little Tartary has no drawn border and sits at the edge of the fitted area, so its outline is rough.

1739 · Johann Matthias Hase, for the Homann Heirs · The Russian Empire and Tartary, great and little

Promised in the title, scarce on the map

Carte generale d'Empire de Russie et de Tartarie grande et petite en Europe et Asie.

The titles promise all Tartary, great and little, yet on the map itself the word is used sparingly and is spelled Tataria, without the first r. It is lettered large only twice: Little Tartary north of the Black Sea, and a shortened Tataric. laid over Manchuria under China. Everywhere else it appears only in small notes naming single peoples as Tartars, while the land is lettered Siberia, Yakutia, Turkestan and the Kalmyks.

The whole sheet at the Library of CongressThis map in the atlas

Laid on the earth by 42 matched places. Left out one at a time, a place lands about 123 km from where it belongs; the worst lands 424 km off. That is the mapmaker's error, kept on purpose.

What is uncertain (9 notes)
  • The Library of Congress scan is dark and small, so the lettering was read on a sharper copy of the same plate at the BnF (Gallica btv1b5963132j).
  • The two copies are different issues: the Gallica copy has a dedication at upper left and the imprint Norib. A. 1739, while this sheet has the French title there and an imprint Norimbergae without a year. A change made to the lettering between the issues would not have been seen, though none was noticed where the two were compared.
  • A search of the whole map body found no Great, Russian, Muscovite, Asiatic or Independent Tartary lettered across Siberia or the steppe. 'Grande' and 'majoris et Asiaticae' appear only in the titles.
  • The large Manchurian word is TATARIC, cut short on the sheet, with no second large word. Whether a full stop follows the C could not be seen.
  • Two readings are still partial: the small Tarta.. by the Volga, whose second line is hidden, and the first letter of PORVTI.
  • The far north-east (Chukchi cape, Kamchatka) and the Tarim towns sit 250 to 430 km off, because the sheet itself is wrong there.
  • The outline for Little Tartary follows the green and red hand colour and the shores; the engraved line under the colour could not be made out on this small scan, and the same green also outlines Poland.
  • The Manchurian word TATARIC has no limit of its own on the sheet; its outline is closed on the west by a judged line between it and the Mongol names, and the Russian border, the coast and Korea do the rest.
  • The west end of Little Tartary lands about 130 km too far west on today's earth, over Moldova, though the sheet stops it at the Dniester; no matched place lies west of the Crimea to steady the bend there.

Other big names in the same country

about 1743 · The Homann firm · Map of Asia

Great Tartary as one colour, Siberia inside it

Recentissima Asiae Delineatio, Qua Imperia, ejus Regna, et Status, Unacum novissimis Russorum detectionibus circa Mare Caspium et Terram Yedso alias…

Homann letters TARTARIA MAGNA, Great Tartary, in the largest letters on the mainland, from the Irtysh to the Pacific, and this copy washes one yellow colour over everything from the Urals and the Caspian to Kamchatka, so that Siberia, the Kalmyk country and Bukhara all sit inside it. The word IMPERIUM RUSSORUM, Empire of the Russians, runs from Europe across the Urals into the same ground, and SIBERIA is lettered just above Tartaria Magna, so Tartary here is a region with Russian Siberia inside it and not a state. Beyond the Amur, inside the green of the Chinese empire, stands TARTARIA CHINENSIS, Chinese Tartary, and north of the Black Sea TARTARIA MINOR, Little Tartary. The Arctic off the Lena is called MARE TARTARICUM and the Circassians are named CIRCASSI TARTARI.

The whole sheet at the Library of Congress

1744 · Johann Matthias Hase · Map of Asia

A Chinese-Tartar kingdom, and peoples called Tatars

ASIA secundum legitimas Projectionis Stereographicae regulas et juxta recentissimas observation. et relationes, explosis aliorum fabulosis…

This sheet has no country called Tartary at all, and it spells the word Tatar, without the first r. The only big name that holds the word is REGNVM SINO TATARIC, the Chinese-Tartar Kingdom, spread from the south of China to the Amur: of the nine parts the title promises, this is the only one with a Tartar name, and it means the empire of China under its Manchu rulers. Everywhere else the word is a name for peoples: Crimean, Kuban, Nogai, Ufa and Bashkir Tatars inside or beside Russia, Khivan and Burut Tatars in the middle, Kokonor and Ordos Tatars by China. The north is SIBERIA and IAKVTIA inside the Russian empire, and inner Asia is shared out among Kalmyks, Eleuths, Bukharia, Turkestan, Mongols and Tibet.

about 1755 · Jean Palairet · Map of Asia

Three Tartaries, named by who rules

A MAP of ASIA with its Principal DIVISIONS by J. Palaret, with several Additions & Improvements by L. Delarochette.

This sheet letters RUSSIAN TARTARY by the lower Volga, INDEPENDENT TARTARY across inner Asia from the Caspian to Tibet, and CHINESE TARTARY in one long curve from the Great Wall to the Amur, with LITTLE TARTARY north of the Black Sea. A table printed on the map spells the scheme out: Russian Tartary is the kingdoms of Kasan and Astrachan and part of Circassia; Independent Tartary is the Kara Kalpaks, Turkestan, the Usbecs and the Kingdom of the Eluts with both Bukarias and both Tibets; Chinese Tartary is the Western and Eastern Monguls and the Tartars of Kokonor. Everything north of these is RUSSIA IN ASIA and SIBERIA, with its provinces named, and the word Tartary is not used there at all. There is no Great Tartary on this sheet: the name only appears with a ruler's or a people's name in front of it.

1772 · Woodman and Mutlow · Map of Asia, cut up as a puzzle

Three Tartarys, cut apart like a puzzle

ASIA, Divided Into Its Empires, Kingdoms and States, with their General Subdivisions. LONDON

This sheet letters the word four times as a country. RUSSIAN TARTARY runs across the yellow Russian country from Tobolsk to the Okhotsk coast, under the name SIBERIA, which is lettered over the same ground further north. CHINESE TARTARY runs across the brown country of the Western and Eastern Mongals, from the Great Wall to the Amur. The bare word TARTARY, in the largest letters, is kept for the uncoloured country between them, from the Caspian to the edge of China, where the sheet also letters KASACCIA HORDA, USBECKS, KHARASM, TURKISTAN, GREAT BUKARIA, LITTLE BUKARIA, KALMUKS and ELUTS. LITTLE TARTARY is a small name north of the Black Sea, and two small notes name peoples: the Tartars of Kokonor and the Mantcheu Tartars who subdued China.

Bowles letters three large Tartaries and gives each a drawn border. Russian Tartary is only the pink country between the Black Sea, the Volga and the Urals; Independent Tartary is the green-edged country from the Caspian to Hami; Chinese Tartary is the ground north of the Great Wall from Mongolia to the Pacific, inside the pink wash of the Chinese empire. A table in the corner lists Tartary as one division of Asia made of Chinese, Independent, 'Tibet or Mogulean' and Russian Tartary, and lists 'Russ. Tartary' again under Russia in Asia beside Siberia.

This small sheet writes Tartary only twice. 1799 · Laurie and Whittle · Map of Asia

Russian, Chinese, and a plain Tartary between

ASIA with ITS ISLANDS, and DIFFERENT REGIONS according to THEIR MODERN DIVISIONS

This London sheet still letters the word across most of inner and north Asia. RUSSIAN TARTARY runs along the south of Russian Asia under SIBERIA, in letters of the same size and with no line between the two. TARTARY alone, in the largest letters, crosses a pink country with a dotted border from the Caspian to the Gobi, and inside it stand the Kasaccia Horda, Usbeck, Kharasm, Turkistan, Great and Little Bukaria, the Kalmuks and the Eluts. CHINESE TARTARY, marked off by the same kind of border and split by the words WESTERN and EASTERN, runs on to the Pacific north of the Great Wall, with the Mongals lettered in both halves; LITTLE TARTARY sits north of the Black Sea and the strait beside Saghalien is the CHANNEL OF TARTARY.

How the dial was made

Each sheet is a Library of Congress picture of a printed map. On every one, between 35 and 126 places were matched by an AI reader to where they really are: river mouths, capes, lakes and towns the mapmaker could have known from report. The sheet was then bent, stiffly, so those places fall as near their true spots as the sheet allows. A stiff bend keeps the map looking like itself, so its mistakes stay visible: an oval Caspian, a Siberia squeezed short, towns from Marco Polo set down by guess.

The boxes mark where the word is lettered, traced on each sheet and carried across with it. The larger outlines mark the ground the sheet gives to each country called Tartary. Where the mapmaker engraved a border line, or the sheet is coloured country by country, the outline follows that and is drawn solid. Where he drew no limit at all, the outline is a reading of how far the lettering reaches, carried to the nearest coast, river or neighbouring name, and is drawn dashed. Hand colour was added copy by copy, so an outline that follows colour is true of this copy only. The sizes count only today's dry land under each outline, and are as rough as the sheet: where a map rests on hearsay, the outline is only as good as the map.

Between two stops the dial fades one sheet into the next; nothing is known about the years in between, and where several maps crowd into a few years the scale is eased apart so each can be reached. No person has checked the matched places, the readings or the outlines yet. The many Tartarys counts every map and book in the atlas that uses each name, and How it was made explains the rest.
